title: Perception, Bias and the Judgement You Think Is Yours
author: Radical Conformity
summary: This article argues that most of what intelligent, capable professionals believe to be true was decided by absorption rather than analysis — inherited from the environment of their formation — and that the longer those foundational assumptions go unexamined, the more dangerous they become as entry points for bad information and bad decisions. The core claim is that experience and analytical sophistication do not automatically correct foundational beliefs; in fact, they often reinforce them, because the more capable your thinking, the more effectively you can defend conclusions you were never fully conscious of reaching. The article situates this problem in a contemporary context where trust in institutions is eroding while misinformation operates at unprecedented scale and sophistication, arguing that unexamined foundational beliefs are precisely the point of entry for deliberately constructed narratives. Astute judgment, the piece concludes, requires periodic return to the assumptions beneath the thinking — most professionals never make that return, and the absence of that return is where confident errors compound.
points: Most foundational beliefs are formed by absorption in the environment of one's formation, not through rigorous analysis, and they feel unquestionable precisely because everyone around you held them too — which means they were never tested.

Experience and analytical sophistication do not automatically correct unexamined foundational beliefs; they often reinforce them, because more capable thinking becomes better at defending conclusions reached before full analytical capacity developed.

Unexamined foundational beliefs are the precise point of entry for misinformation: bad information doesn't need to overcome good thinking — it only needs to find an assumption that was never questioned and confirm it.

In an environment where narratives are constructed and distributed with precision at unprecedented scale, the professional who has never audited their own foundational assumptions is the most reliably exploitable target.

Astute judgment requires periodic return to the assumptions beneath the thinking — most people never make that return, and the decisions built on unexamined foundations feel considered even when they are not.
quotes: Most of what you believe to be true was decided a long time ago. Not through rigorous analysis. Through absorption. You grew up inside a set of assumptions about how the world works, who can be trusted, what institutions exist to do, and what is broadly true.
The problem is not that those assumptions were formed. That is unavoidable. The problem is that most of them have never been seriously retested.

The assumption that they can be trusted without scrutiny, simply because they once seemed trustworthy, is a different matter entirely. That assumption belongs to an earlier version of you, formed before you had the full capability to examine it.

In that environment, unexamined foundational beliefs are not a minor liability. They are the precise point of entry for bad information. Misinformation does not need to overcome good thinking. It only needs to find an assumption that was never questioned and confirm it.

Experience and capability do not automatically correct this. In many cases they reinforce it. The more sophisticated your thinking, the more effectively you can defend conclusions you were never fully conscious of reaching.

Astute judgement requires more than good current thinking. It requires periodic return to the assumptions beneath the thinking. Most people never make that return. The foundations hold, and the decisions built on top of them feel considered.
